addedResources.name: M/M/1 queue - model definition and stationary analysis
addedResources.use: Read Model definition (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, single server, infinite buffer, FIFO) and Stationary analysis (stability lambda < mu, rho = lambda/mu, L = rho/(1 - rho), response time 1/(mu - lambda) via Little's Law). Use the closed forms as approximations with assumptions stated, checked by your own simulation.

study.title: Sampling: head versus tail
study.locator: Terminology (sampled versus not sampled); Head Sampling (decision from trace ID before the outcome); Tail Sampling (error and latency criteria; stateful operating cost)

focus: White-box metrics expose internals and imminent failure; black-box checks prove user-visible symptoms. Page on symptoms, debug with causes.
One label-value combination is one stored series. At 3 services x 5 endpoints x 3 codes x 4 instances the metric holds 180 series; adding a 200,000-value user label takes it to 9,000,000.
Head sampling decides from the trace ID before the outcome is known, so it cannot keep every error. Tail sampling waits for completed spans and pays stateful cost.
Keep what the Programming unit enforced: bounded label values, no secrets in attributes, and raw records retained behind every aggregate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the series count for labels service (3 values), endpoint (5), status (3) and instance (4): 180. Add user_id with 200,000 values: 9,000,000. State which label breaks the budget and give the bounded replacement: drop user_id from the metric and keep it on sampled traces only.
traps: Treating a shared request ID as proof of causation. Sampling, retries and shared queues break the causal reading; the ID joins evidence, it does not assign blame.
Putting request IDs, user IDs or tokens in metric labels. Each new value mints new series, and secrets in labels leak into every backend that stores them.
Averaging a histogram across services and reading the result as a percentile. Percentiles come from pooled raw samples, never from averaged summaries.

selfTest.q: When should a page come from black-box rather than white-box monitoring?
selfTest.a: When the condition is already user-visible and urgent. White-box predicts or explains; black-box proves the symptom. Every page stays urgent, actionable and needing intelligence.

selfTest.q: A metric has labels with 3, 5, 3 and 4 values. How many series? What happens when a 200,000-value label is added?
selfTest.a: 180 series; then 9,000,000. Collection, storage and query cost scale with series count, so the unbounded label must move to sampled traces or logs.

selfTest.q: Why can head sampling miss every error in a release?
selfTest.a: Its decision uses the trace ID before the outcome exists. Keeping all errors needs tail sampling, which waits for completed spans and pays stateful cost.

selfTest.q: Two services report the same averaged p99. Can you rank them?
selfTest.a: No. Averaged quantiles are not the quantile of the pooled data. Recompute from retained raw samples with their sample sizes.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the instrumented request path (request ID, queue wait, handler time, storage time, status, bounded labels) with local export, raw record retention and an enforced cardinality budget.

outcomes: Define latency, throughput, goodput, utilization and saturation, and separate queue wait from service time.
Report p50, p95 and p99 from raw samples with the sample size, and explain what the mean hides.
Measure a load sweep on your machine and name the saturated resource with its utilization.
units.why: Every SLO and capacity number later in this section reads a latency distribution. Assumed background: the Programming profiling-benchmarking unit, which built benchmark harnesses; this unit makes their output honest, with distributions first and one-number summaries never.

next.note: Turn the measured wait into concurrency and capacity math.

study.title: Saturation and served-traffic metrics
study.locator: Metrics with Purpose (Saturation: track every resource, hard limits and degradation thresholds; Status of Served Traffic: break down by status and quota denial)

focus: Latency is a distribution. The SRE example (mean 100 ms, 1% at 5 s) and the Figure 4-1 bands show why one mean plus one threshold cannot describe user experience.

Goodput counts useful completions; throughput counts all completions; errors by policy can turn slow successes into failures. Saturation is the fraction of the most constrained resource, and most systems degrade before 100%.
Separate service time from queue wait in every measurement. Utilization explains which one dominates.
Percentiles need raw samples and n. Report n with the value, never a bare p99.
units.reproduce: Run this seeded script with /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I (CPython 3.14.4; seed 7 makes it reproducible on any machine; checked on Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K): 5000 samples, 2% from N(400, 80) ms else N(40, 8) ms, clipped at 1 ms, nearest-rank percentiles. Confirm n=5000, mean 48.19 ms, p50 40.16 ms, p95 55.16 ms, p99 421.05 ms, max 627.33 ms. Then explain why a dashboard showing mean 48 ms and p95 55 ms still hides about 100 requests above 400 ms.
traps: Averaging percentiles from shards or windows. The two halves here give p95 54.84 and 55.45 ms; only the pooled computation is the p95.
Mixing failed-request latency into success latency, or dropping it. Fast 500s flatter the mean while slow errors are worse than fast ones; track both.
Reading 60% average utilization as headroom. The saturated resource is the most constrained one; queue wait grows on its utilization, not the average.

selfTest.q: Mean 48 ms and p95 55 ms over 5000 requests. How many exceed 400 ms?
selfTest.a: About 100. The p99 is 421.05 ms, so at least 50 exceed 421 ms, and the 2% slow mixture puts roughly 100 above 400 ms. Count from samples, never from the mean.

selfTest.q: 100 rps with 5% errors and 10% of requests retried once: throughput versus goodput?
selfTest.a: Throughput counts completions (100 rps plus 10 retry rps of load). Goodput counts first-try useful completions (95 rps). Retries add load without adding goodput.

selfTest.q: Utilization reads 85% but latency is flat. Saturated?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. Saturation is about the most constrained resource and its queue. Check queue wait, queue depth, the 99th percentile trend and per-resource utilization.
Latency spans orders of magnitude. Factor-of-3 buckets resolve both the 40 ms body and the 400 ms tail without storing every sample.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a load sweep through saturation on the learner's service reporting p50, p95 and p99 from retained raw samples with n, plus throughput, goodput, queue depth, utilization, errors and recovery.

study.title: Burn-rate alert shapes
study.locator: Ways to Alert on Significant Events (Alert on Burn Rate; Multiwindow, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts)
study.depth: Read for alert-shape vocabulary only. Alert implementation belongs to the incidents unit.

focus: SLI is good events over total events; SLO is the target; the error budget is 100% minus the SLO times the window event count.
A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows 43.2 minutes of full outage; over 3 million requests it allows 3,000 errors. The same budget reads both ways.
Series availability multiplies (0.999 x 0.995 = 0.99401) only for independent failures. Shared power, zones or deploys break the multiplication.
RPO bounds data loss (backup freshness); RTO bounds downtime (restore plus failover). MTBF 720 h with MTTR 1 h gives 0.99861, and holding 0.999 needs MTTR at most 0.72072 h.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 30-day 99.9% budget (30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes), the series product 0.999 x 0.995 = 0.99401 with independence stated, and the MTBF/MTTR pair 720/721 = 0.99861 with maximum MTTR 720 x 0.001/0.999 = 0.72072 h. Then state the RPO check a restore drill must pass: the newest restorable record is no older than the RPO.
traps: A 100% SLO. Change itself is the top outage source, so 100% forbids deploys and leaves no room to improve.
Setting the SLO from current performance. It locks in heroic effort or hides user pain; start loose and tighten with evidence.
Quoting availability without the window and without independence. 99.9% over a week is 10.1 minutes, not 43.2.

selfTest.q: 3 million requests in 4 weeks at 99.9% availability: budget? One outage caused 1500 errors: share?
selfTest.a: 3,000 errors; the outage spent 50% of the budget.

selfTest.q: Two replicas at 0.99 each share one rack power feed. Combined availability?
selfTest.a: Not 0.9999. The independence assumption fails; the shared feed makes it one failure near 0.99.

selfTest.q: RPO is 1 hour and the last verified backup is 90 minutes old. Pass?
selfTest.a: No. Freshness exceeds RPO, so restore would lose up to 90 minutes. Take and verify a new backup.

selfTest.q: A burn-rate alert fires while the window SLO dashboard is green. What does that mean?
selfTest.a: Budget is being consumed fast relative to the window. The multiwindow alert predicts exhaustion before the window average moves.
